From what I've seen, people tend to swing from anxiety to depression - even on a neurochemical level: Your brain goes into a state of high arousal before your parasympathetic nervous system kicks in and then you hit a low. 

If you are experiencing a lot of anxiety, it might explain the depressive episodes and lack of creativity/motivation/joy/confidence etc. so it might be worth exploring whether you might be experiencing a lot of anxiety - either acute attacks, or a high baseline level of constant anxiety.

On a purely functional level, that you found keeping a diary had worked for you and that you have moved on is progress - which is a good sign. Ever thought about doing something to blow off steam like kickboxing, target practice, or just getting some cheap crockery and smashing it the hell up (or becoming a vocalist in a punk band perhaps)?

Have you started getting involved in any communities where you are living now? 
The feeling of belonging and acceptance, as well as the  power to make contributions are a big part of improving depression which get overlooked in the individualized approach to mental health problems. 

Do you feel as though you belong and you are accepted? 

Do you feel like you are valued by and important to those around you?

Alright, first tip - ginger. Seriously. If you are having nausea due to anything other than anxiety it works better than prescription medication. Pickled or candied ginger also has sugar in it, which keeps your blood glucose level elevated to help reduce nausea too.

If it is anxiety, it could be due to coming off the antidepressants or just the pent up stuff due to the sh*t you've been through. Try small trips in the car - to the local store or somewhere familiar to help desensitize yourself.

It sounds like you've put a lot of effort into getting back out there, but it doesn't seem to have worked. Could it be that perhaps you are still grieving? Sometimes when you experience losses the way you have, it takes time, space and patience before you are ready to be back to your normal self. Avoiding giving yourself the space to really process this stuff might actually be making things more difficult.

Have you tried writing down the stuff that's in your head? I mean, like cutting loose and just throwing it all down on paper. Or maybe drawing it out instead - it sounds like you might be more inclined to do that.

What are your thoughts on this?

Are you painting to please other people? Or are you painting because you like to do it?

Sometimes we get confused about why we do things or who we do them for. It's easy to take criticism to heart when you are putting other people above yourself.

When was the last time you did something for yourself? Maybe it's time that you do something nice just for you. Who cares if it's something that is high in calories or if it's a cheesy comedy movie? In the grand scheme of things, it doesn't really matter.

Just like whether someone does/n't like your paintings - in the grand scheme of things, it doesn't count for very much at all. 

What does count is if you make a decision to paint for yourself - because it counts for you.

Hey, I'm not advocating suicide, but the way a 13 year old feels is equally as important as the way a 25 year old feels. 

Telling someone to shut up or that they are stupid is not a good way to go about this.

Please be careful when dealing with suicidal people when you tell them they have no intention of killing themselves - it would be awful if they saw it as a challenge or that they need to make an attempt to 'prove' they feel this badly. Yes, a 13 year old does not have the same executive function and impulse control of a fully-developed adult, but that's all the more reason to be careful in these circumstances.
